{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nc-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"b160989dcfabe6117f31bcb3d1dbbff761e8b194204d6c93f4fcb83e16f1e77d","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nc-class-c:lineage:23","source_registry_sha256":"e128656a3d00ba5437556728ebd87f5842c83601163739613417fe77cf9f423b","source_liveness_sha256":"dbfdf3e6d892a41c42c05809a9213d44a78aedd480dc6de23937c97292428b74"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Driver condition and occupant protection","heading":"C — Driver condition, drowsy and distracted driving, cell phone law, alcohol effects, seat belts, child restraints, air bags and helmets (North Carolina)","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Driver condition, drowsy and distracted driving, cell phone law, alcohol effects, seat belts, child restraints, air bags and helmets (North Carolina)
Knowledge domain: what makes a driver unfit to drive safely, the North Carolina phone rules, and the laws and practices that protect drivers, passengers, children and riders.

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Both physical and mental health shape how you drive, and a driver license requires that you be in good health. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
Even a short illness such as a cold, a headache or the flu can leave you less alert and slower to respond behind the wheel. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
At 55 mph a vehicle covers the length of a football field in 3.7 seconds, so even a brief nod-off is dangerous. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
Crashes caused by drowsiness tend to be serious and happen most often on fast rural highways when the driver is traveling alone. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
Signs of drowsiness include not remembering the last few miles, hitting a rumble strip or drifting out of your lane, yawning again and again, and struggling to focus or keep your eyes open. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
If you grow tired while driving you should stop; a nap of 15 to 45 minutes and some caffeine help only for a while. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
On a long drive, take a break at least every 2 hours: leave the car, stretch and walk briskly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A02
The handbook suggests capping your driving at about 300 to 400 miles a day and avoiding medicines that make you drowsy. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A02
Distracted driving means any activity that might pull your attention away from the main job of driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A02
Common distractions include texting, phone use, eating or drinking, talking with passengers, grooming, reading maps, using navigation, watching video and adjusting audio equipment. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A02
Distracted drivers respond more slowly to events such as a car slowing to turn or pulling out of a side road, and they miss hazards like pedestrians or debris more often. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A02
Many distractions make it harder to steer clear of a crash because they take at least one hand off the steering wheel. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A02
North Carolina makes it unlawful to text or email on a cell phone while driving on a public street, highway or public vehicular area. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A02
A driver under 18 may not use a cell phone or related technology at all while the vehicle is moving, except to call 911 in an emergency. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A02
No one may drive a school bus on a public road or vehicular area while using a cell phone or other mobile-device technology. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A02
Use a phone while driving only when truly necessary, for emergencies or to reach a parent, legal guardian or spouse, and only at a safe time and place. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A03
Let a passenger make the call for you, let unanswered calls go to a message, and secure the phone so it cannot fly around in a crash. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A03
Both prescription and over-the-counter medicines can affect driving, so learn how a medicine affects you and drive as little as possible while taking it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A03
The handbook states that about 38 percent of all traffic deaths involve alcohol. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A03
Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain, so you cannot respond, decide or react quickly. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A03
Alcohol weakens your judgment of speed and of distance to other cars, people or objects, and gives false confidence that leads to bigger risks. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A03
Alcohol makes it hard to handle more than one task, so while steering you may miss traffic lights, cars from side streets or pedestrians; it also upsets balance and causes sleepiness. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A03
Only time sobers a drinker; coffee, a large meal or a cold shower will not. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A03
Ways to avoid drinking and driving include planning a ride in advance, sharing a taxi, taking public transit, staying overnight with a friend, or riding with someone who has not been drinking. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A04
Across a typical lifetime behind the wheel, the odds of a serious injury or death in a crash are roughly one in three. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A04
In a vehicle built with seat belts, the driver and every passenger must wear a properly fastened belt whenever the vehicle moves forward on a North Carolina street or highway. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A04
Seat belts are still required in vehicles with air bags, and if the vehicle has automatic shoulder harnesses the lap belt must also be worn. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A04
The seat belt law exempts an occupant of a noncommercial vehicle whose medical or physical condition, or professionally certified phobia, prevents proper restraint. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A04
Rural letter carriers of the Postal Service on duty and newspaper carriers delivering along their route are exempt from the seat belt law. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A04
Drivers or passengers who keep stopping to leave the vehicle or deliver items are exempt if the vehicle goes no faster than 20 mph between stops. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A04
Other exemptions cover property-carrying vehicles used for farming within the state, vehicles not legally required to have belts, and situations where every belted or restraint-equipped seat is already taken. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A04
In a motor home, occupants other than the driver and front-seat passengers are exempt when the motor home has at least four of the listed living facilities. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A05
Correctly used safety seats could save seven of every 10 children who die while riding unrestrained. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A05
The best child seat is one used on every ride that fits your car and has a comfortable harness or shield, and low-cost rentals are often offered by local groups, hospitals and health departments. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F35 | anchor: A05
A driver carrying any passenger under 16 must make sure each one is secured in a child restraint or seat belt meeting the federal standards in force when it was made. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F36 | anchor: A05
A child younger than 8 who weighs under 80 pounds must ride in a weight-appropriate child passenger restraint. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F37 | anchor: A05
When a vehicle has an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat, a child under 5 weighing under 40 pounds must ride in the rear unless the restraint is built for use with a front air bag. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F38 | anchor: A05
If no seat has a lap and shoulder belt for the restraint, a child under 8 weighing 40 to 80 pounds may ride with a properly fitted lap belt alone. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F39 | anchor: A05
Children who have outgrown safety seats should use federally compliant booster seats until an adult belt fits: lap belt snug on the hips, not the stomach, and shoulder belt across the shoulder and chest, not the face or throat. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F40 | anchor: A05
An air bag bursts out of the dashboard at up to 200 mph, faster than an eye blink, so it is far from a soft pillow. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F41 | anchor: A06
Children aged 12 and younger should ride buckled up in a rear seat. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F42 | anchor: A06
An infant in a rear-facing safety seat must never ride in the front seat of a vehicle that has a passenger-side air bag. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F43 | anchor: A06
Air bags only supplement belts: wear the lap belt under the abdomen and low on the hips, and the shoulder belt over the collarbone, away from the neck and across the breastbone. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F44 | anchor: A06
Move the driver and front passenger seats as far back as practical, especially for shorter people. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F45 | anchor: A06
Every motorcycle or moped operator and passenger must wear a safety helmet meeting Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 218. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F46 | anchor: A06
A compliant helmet has a firm polystyrene liner about one inch thick and a DOT symbol fixed permanently on the back by the maker; a sticker added later does not make it legal. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F47 | anchor: A06
North Carolina bars children younger than 16 from riding in the open bed of a pickup truck, and the driver is responsible for compliance, though the statute has some exemptions. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

Misconceptions: air bags do not replace seat belts, they only supplement them; coffee or a cold shower does not sober a drinker; the under-eighteen phone rule bans all phone use while moving apart from emergency calls, not just texting; a loose DOT sticker does not make a novelty helmet legal; a short nap is a temporary fix, not a cure for fatigue.
Mnemonics: belts first, bags second; kids in back; only time sobers; tired means stop.
Glossary: drowsy driving means driving while sleepy enough to lose focus; distracted driving means any activity taking attention from driving; child passenger restraint means a crash-tested child safety seat; booster seat means a seat raising a child so the adult belt fits; open bed means a cargo area without permanent overhead structure.
Dynamic facts: phone, seat belt, child restraint and helmet rules are set by statute and can change, and rental-seat programs vary by community; confirm with current North Carolina law.
